story: The Permafrost Discovery Gateway's near real time Arctic lake drainage tracker and the roughly 30 northwestern Alaska lakes it flagged in June and July 2026

claims.claim: Researchers found around 30 more lakes that were affected by drainage in June and July 2026.
claims.verbatim: We found around 30 more lakes that were affected by drainage in June and July 2026.
claims.notes: Bylined by the two researchers who did the work. Opinion and analysis format, not peer reviewed. Keep the hedge, around 30, never 30 exactly.

claims.claim: The Seward and Baldwin peninsulas in northwestern Alaska are described by the researchers as hot spots for lakes suddenly draining.
claims.verbatim: The Seward and Baldwin peninsulas in northwestern Alaska are hot spots for lakes suddenly draining.
claims.notes: Northwestern Alaska and the two named peninsulas are the same place. The around 30 count belongs to this one region.

claims.claim: The researchers write that although winter 2025 to 26 was on the cold side for Alaska, the region continued to lose lake area.
claims.verbatim: Although winter 2025-26 was on the cold side for Alaska, this region continued to lose lake area
claims.notes: The cold winter characterization is the authors' own. On the cold side is a hedge, not a measured anomaly. Do not upgrade to a temperature figure.

claims.claim: The authors say the continued loss of lake area suggests evidence of permafrost thaw.
claims.verbatim: this region continued to lose lake area – suggesting evidence of permafrost thaw
claims.notes: The authors say suggesting, not proving. A slide that hardens this overstates the source.

claims.claim: In the summer of 2018 alone almost 200 of the region's approximately 4,600 lakes lost more than a quarter of their area.
claims.verbatim: In the summer of 2018 alone, almost 200 of the region's approximately 4,600 lakes lost more than a quarter of their area
claims.notes: Both figures live in one sentence. Print the source's hedges, almost 200 and approximately 4,600, and more than a quarter rather than 25 percent.

claims.claim: Over the past two decades the region lost many large lakes that had covered its landscape for thousands of years.
claims.verbatim: Over the past two decades, this region lost many large lakes that had covered its landscape for thousands of years.
claims.notes: Qualitative, many, with no count attached. Do not attach a number. This is what makes 2026 a continuation rather than an event.

claims.claim: An international team working through the Permafrost Discovery Gateway has mapped and now actively monitors over 4 million lakes across the Arctic.
claims.verbatim: An international team of scientists we work with through the Permafrost Discovery Gateway has mapped and now actively monitors over 4 million lakes across the Arctic
claims.notes: ARCTIC WIDE, not Alaska. Over 4 million, so more than 4 million is fair and an exact 4,000,000 is not.

claims.claim: The same mapping covers 70 million thermokarst ponds, also known as trough ponds, across the Alaska tundra.
claims.verbatim: 70 million thermokarst ponds – also known as trough ponds – across the Alaska tundra.
claims.notes: ALASKA TUNDRA ONLY, unlike C07 which is Arctic wide. Never add the two together.

claims.claim: When ice rich permafrost thaws the ground surface subsides, creating thermokarst ponds, which the authors describe as depressions that fill with water.
claims.verbatim: When ice-rich permafrost thaws, the ground surface subsides, creating what are known as thermokarst ponds – depressions that fill with water.
claims.notes: The mechanism sentence the deck's argument rests on. The water arrives because the ice left.

claims.claim: The authors say the same process that starts the sinkhole can form new stream channels that drain the lake, leaving a circular basin of bare ground behind.
claims.verbatim: Sometimes, the same process that started the sinkhole can form new stream channels that drain the lake, leaving a circular basin of bare ground behind.
claims.notes: The visible artifact, and the source names its shape as circular. Strong art brief.

claims.claim: The authors write that a lake several hundred meters long might have taken a millennium to form yet permafrost thaw triggered by one unusually warm summer can completely drain it in just a few hours.
claims.value: a millennium to form, a few hours to drain
claims.verbatim: A lake that is several hundred meters long might have taken a millennium to form, yet permafrost thaw triggered by one unusually warm summer can completely drain the same lake in just a few hours.
claims.notes: A characteristic case, not a measured single event. Keep the hedges might have and can.

claims.claim: The authors state that not all lake changes are caused by permafrost thaw.
claims.verbatim: However, not all lake changes are caused by permafrost thaw.
claims.notes: THE CAVEAT, and it is load bearing. The only limitation passage in the article. It gets its own slide.

claims.claim: The authors note that lakes in floodplains and wetlands change dramatically across each season due to the abundance of snowmelt water in spring, and that wildlife can also play a role.
claims.verbatim: it is not uncommon that lakes in floodplains and wetlands change dramatically across each season due to the abundance of snowmelt water in spring. Wildlife can also play a role.
claims.notes: The named confounders behind C12. Wildlife is the authors' word, so do not name beavers on a slide.

claims.claim: Aerial photos starting from the late 1940s and satellite imagery that became available in the 1970s have helped scientists map what the Arctic's permafrost landscapes looked like.
claims.verbatim: Aerial photos starting from the late 1940s and satellite imagery that became available in the 1970s have helped scientists map what the Arctic's permafrost landscapes looked like
claims.notes: Write late 1940s, not 1948 or 1949.

claims.claim: The authors write that Arctic temperatures rise at two to three times the global average rate.
claims.verbatim: temperatures there rise at two to three times the global average rate.
claims.notes: A conservative statement of a contested range. Attribute to the authors rather than stating it flatly.

claims.claim: The authors say the new maps can show where land is underlain by ice rich permafrost, meaning bad choices for building sites, and where the frozen soil has less ice, likely indicating it is safer for building.
claims.verbatim: The new maps can show where land is underlain by ice-rich permafrost, meaning bad choices for building sites, and where the frozen soil has less ice, likely indicating it's safer for building sites.
claims.notes: What the tool is for. The asymmetry is the point, it is more confident about where not to build than about where to build.

claims.claim: The authors say detecting signs of permafrost thaw in those landscapes can help communities plan for changes to their environment.
claims.verbatim: Detecting signs of permafrost thaw in those landscapes can help communities plan for changes to their environment.
claims.notes: Who the instrument is for, in the authors' own words. Communities, not agencies.

claims.claim: On August 13th, 2026 the Permafrost Discovery Gateway launched a new tool that allows users to explore lake drainage across the Arctic.
claims.verbatim: On August 13, 2026, the Permafrost Discovery Gateway launched a new tool that allows users to explore lake drainage across the Arctic.
claims.notes: THE NEWS PEG. Verified, but single sourced and NOT from The Conversation piece, which states no launch date. Attribute on the slide to Woodwell Climate.

claims.claim: Woodwell Climate says that for the first time ever users can track lake drainage associated with ice rich permafrost thaw in near real time and across the entire Arctic region.
claims.verbatim: For the first time ever, users can track lake drainage associated with ice-rich permafrost thaw in near-real time, and across the entire Arctic region.
claims.notes: A first party priority claim. Print as attributed speech or drop the priority clause and keep the capability.

claims.claim: Woodwell Climate describes the Permafrost Discovery Gateway as an online platform in development for creating, analyzing and visualizing big geospatial permafrost products.
claims.verbatim: Permafrost Discovery Gateway is an online platform in development for creating, analyzing, and visualizing big geospatial permafrost products to enable knowledge-generation about the changing Arctic landscape.
claims.notes: In development is the operators' own phrase and the counterweight to C19. Do not call this a finished instrument.

claims.claim: NCEAS says the Permafrost Discovery Gateway is a resource where the only thing you need is a web browser and internet to get access to scientific products.
claims.verbatim: The Permafrost Discovery Gateway is a resource, a tool online that the only thing you need is a web browser and internet and then you can get access to scientific products
claims.source_outlet: National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis, UC Santa Barbara
claims.notes: BACKGROUND, March 2026. No named speaker was attributable, so do not set it in quotation marks beside a person's name.

claims.claim: NCEAS reports that in Alaska alone roughly 80 percent of the land contains permafrost to some degree and more than 140 communities build on it.
claims.verbatim: In Alaska alone, roughly 80 percent of the land contains permafrost to some degree, and more than 140 communities build on it.
claims.source_outlet: National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis, UC Santa Barbara
claims.notes: ALASKA communities, not Arctic. A scout returned Arctic and that would have printed an error. BACKGROUND, March 2026. Keep to some degree, which includes discontinuous and sporadic permafrost.

claims.claim: Anna Liljedahl is bylined as Affiliated Professor in Arctic Hydrology at the University of Alaska Fairbanks.
claims.verbatim: Anna Liljedahl, Affiliated Professor in Arctic Hydrology, University of Alaska Fairbanks
claims.notes: A specific affiliate title. The deck must not imply UAF ran this work.

claims.claim: Woodwell Climate Research Center lists Anna Liljedahl as an Associate Scientist.
claims.verbatim: Anna Liljedahl, Associate Scientist
claims.notes: No conflict with C23. If the deck names one institution, name Woodwell and put the UAF affiliation second.

claims.claim: Ingmar Nitze is bylined as a postdoctoral researcher in polar geoscience at the Alfred Wegener Institute.
claims.verbatim: Ingmar Nitze, Postdoctoral Research in Polar Geoscience, Alfred Wegener Institute
claims.notes: The byline string reads Postdoctoral Research, apparently a typo on the page. The claim writes researcher rather than reproducing it. Full institution name is Alfred Wegener Institute Helmholtz Centre for Polar and Marine Research.

claims.claim: Anna Liljedahl discloses funding from the Google.org Impact Challenge on Climate Innovation, the National Science Foundation under awards 1927872, 2052107 and 2234117, and Woodwell Climate Research Center.
claims.verbatim: Anna Liljedahl receives funding from Google.org Impact Challenge on Climate Innovation, the National Science Foundation (Awards #1927872, 2052107, 2234117), and Woodwell Climate Research Center.
claims.notes: A personal funding disclosure, which is not identical to what funds the Gateway. Do not write NSF funded the tracker on this basis alone.

claims.claim: Ingmar Nitze discloses funding from Google.org Impact Challenge on Climate Innovation, the National Science Foundation, the Schmidt Sciences Virtual Institute for the Carbon Cycle and the Alfred Wegener Institute.
claims.verbatim: Ingmar Nitze receives funding from Google.org Impact Challenge on Climate Innovation, the National Science Foundation, Schmidt Sciences Virtual Institute for the Carbon Cycle (VICC), and the Alfred Wegener Institute Helmholtz Centre for Polar and Marine Research.
claims.notes: Both authors name Google.org first. Nitze's NSF line carries no award numbers.

claims.claim: Woodwell Climate was awarded a five million dollar Google.org grant for use of AI to track permafrost thaw.
claims.verbatim: Woodwell Climate awarded $5M Google.org grant for use of AI to track permafrost thaw
claims.notes: Amount and recipient confirmed. THE YEAR IS NOT. A slide must not supply one.

claims.claim: NCEAS reported in March 2026 that the Permafrost Discovery Gateway is supported in part by Google.org but that the funding is coming to an end.
claims.verbatim: The Permafrost Discovery Gateway is currently supported in part by Google.org, but that funding is coming to an end.
claims.source_outlet: National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis, UC Santa Barbara
claims.notes: MUST BE DATE STAMPED. A March 2026 statement with no amount, no end date and no named speaker, and the August launch happened after it. Never write the funding is ending.

claims.claim: The article was published on August 26th, 2026 and updated on August 27th, 2026.
claims.verbatim: Published: August 26, 2026 8:39am EDT Updated: August 27, 2026 2:17pm EDT
claims.notes: Two days inside the run window. Live news, not background.

claims.claim: Alaska Beacon republished the article under the same headline with a feed timestamp of August 28th, 2026.
claims.verbatim: Disappearing lakes and AI are helping scientists map Arctic permafrost thaw in near-real time
claims.notes: The article page 403s automated fetchers, so this was verified through the site's RSS feed. Establishes the story landed in Alaska press.

claims.claim: Phys.org carried the article on August 26th, 2026 under a headline that adds old photos to the title.
claims.verbatim: Disappearing lakes, old photos and AI are helping scientists map Arctic permafrost thaw in near-real time
claims.notes: An independent second fetch confirming C01, C05 and C07.

dropped.assertion: More than 140 ARCTIC communities are built on permafrost.
dropped.why_dropped: Wrong on the facts. NCEAS says in Alaska alone, roughly 80 percent of the land contains permafrost to some degree, and more than 140 communities build on it. It is ALASKA communities. Replaced by C22.
The amount and recipient verify, the YEAR does not. Kept without a year as C28.

dropped.assertion: The Gateway currently monitors 4 million lakes and 70 million ponds as shown on its live portal.
dropped.why_dropped: Could not verify against the portal. Both permafrost.arcticdata.io and arcticdata.io/catalog/portals/permafrost return a client side shell reading Loading. The figures survive as C07 and C08, sourced to the authors and not to the running instrument.

dropped.assertion: The tracker updates weekly or on a stated cadence as new satellite passes arrive.
dropped.why_dropped: Not in any source. The article says near real time and never defines a refresh interval. No cadence goes on a slide.

dropped.assertion: The system uses Sentinel or Landsat imagery and a named deep learning model.
dropped.why_dropped: Not present. The article names no satellite and no model architecture. Both scouts' technical detail here was inferred.

dropped.assertion: Around 30 lakes drained completely in June and July 2026.
dropped.why_dropped: Overstates the source, which says affected by drainage, not fully drained. Corrected as C01.

dropped.assertion: The cold 2025-26 winter proves permafrost thaw is now self sustaining and independent of air temperature.
dropped.why_dropped: Not in any source and not supported by one. Scout interpretation, and the exact kind of hardening that must not reach a slide.

dropped.assertion: Anna Liljedahl is a professor at the University of Alaska Fairbanks.
dropped.why_dropped: Materially wrong by omission. Her UAF title is Affiliated Professor in Arctic Hydrology and her employer is Woodwell Climate. Split into C23 and C24.

dropped.assertion: The Permafrost Discovery Gateway is a finished, fully public Alaska instrument.
dropped.why_dropped: Contradicted by its own operators, who call it an online platform in development. See C20.

notes: NEWS PEG. The August 13th, 2026 launch is verified but single sourced, from Woodwell Climate's own project page, not from The Conversation piece, which states no launch date. arcticdata.io would have been the independent confirmation and is a client side shell. Attribute the peg to Woodwell Climate on the slide. TWO GEOGRAPHY TRAPS. Northwestern Alaska and the Seward and Baldwin peninsulas are the same place, and the around 30 count belongs to that one region. The two headline counts have different footprints, over 4 million lakes is ARCTIC WIDE and 70 million thermokarst ponds is ALASKA TUNDRA ONLY. Never add them. THE 140 CORRECTION. Alaska communities, not Arctic. THE CAVEAT IS MANDATORY. C12 and C13 are the article's only limitation passage and the deck gives them a slide, not a line of small type. Beyond that passage the authors state no accuracy figure, no false positive rate, no validation method and no resolution limit, which is itself a limit the deck names in its own voice. SOFTENING FLAGS. C19 for the first time ever is a first party priority claim. C29 is a March 2026 statement about funding with no amount and no end date, and the August launch happened after it. C15 two to three times is a conservative statement of a contested range. C04 keeps suggesting and never proving. 24 of 32 claims are primary and all 32 carry a fetched source URL.
